paragraphs: Here's what I want you to hold onto, friend. The same miracle sent people two ways. Some saw what Jesus did and believed in Him (John 11:45). Others took the same news to the Pharisees (John 11:46). Seeing a dead man walk out of a tomb didn't settle anything by itself, so what you do with what you've seen matters.

Now look at Caiaphas. The council was scared of losing "our place and our nation" (John 11:48), and Caiaphas said it was better that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish (John 11:50). He meant it as a cold bit of math. But John tells us Caiaphas did not say this on his own, and that he was prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation, and for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one (John 11:51-52). The council set out to kill Him, and God was still the One working out what would happen (John 11:53).

So you can trust this, baker. The leaders gave orders to turn anybody who knew where Jesus was into a lookout (John 11:57), and Jesus still stayed the course. He stepped away for a while, and nobody's plot rewrote what He came to do (John 11:54). Jesus isn't scrambling and He isn't caught off guard. I think that's the best news in the whole passage, and it's why I keep my ovens warm. This story isn't over, and there's more still to come.
